title: Researching Experience Over Time
editorial_note: Opening revised to lead with the lesson itself. Remaining dialogue is an automated editorial draft; review spoken wording and meaning before final publication.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Researching Experience Over Time.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Some questions cannot be answered in a single session. Diary studies, longitudinal research, and in-the-wild methods reveal habits, recurrence, learning, abandonment, changing context, and the difference between first impression and sustained value. They are useful when the product depends on a rhythm: health, money, travel, collaboration, notifications, or behaviour change.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at analyse trajectories and attrition?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Researchers build individual timelines before comparing cases. They distinguish product events, external changes, participant interpretation, and outcome. Patterns include stable monitoring, escalating contact, constraint change, successful alternative, and silent abandonment.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: People who stop contributing may be overburdened, unwell, dissatisfied, or simply resolved; attrition is both a validity issue and possible product evidence, investigated without pressure.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Accumulated diary data is highly identifying. The team minimises detail, limits access, reconfirms use, and defines deletion. Findings do not estimate prevalence; validated telemetry and survey evidence later examine reach.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at capture change, waiting, and resumption?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Time-based evidence reveals how understanding and trust change, where people create reminders, and which uncertainties become harmful only after delay. Attrition and missing entries are analysed rather than treated as neutral. Diary reports are compared with service events and follow-up interviews to interpret what occurred.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at failure modes in practice?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Calendar-led cadence: prompts follow researcher convenience instead of meaningful events. Research-created habit: frequent reminders cause the behavior the study claims to observe. Survivor story: only diligent completers shape the conclusion. Smooth journey fiction: loops, regression, and changing goals are edited into one linear path.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Accumulating exposure: sensitive longitudinal data grows without renewed minimisation or consent.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Plan a manageable cadence. Ask people to record specific events close to when they occur, collect relevant artifacts where appropriate, and check in to clarify patterns without turning the study into a burden. Expect incomplete entries; design the study around meaningful incidents rather than constant reporting.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at choose a temporal method?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Journeys involving learning, habit, health, finance, waiting, trust, or repeated service use cannot be understood in one session. Use diaries, experience sampling, longitudinal interviews, repeated usability, telemetry, or cohort analysis according to the question. Define duration and prompt frequency around meaningful events without creating excessive burden.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Capture episodes close to occurrence through short entries, media, artefacts, or event-triggered questions. Follow up to understand interpretation and change. Track context, interruptions, workarounds, adaptation, and dropout. Participants who remain may differ from those who stop, so attrition is evidence and a validity concern.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Protect privacy as data accumulates; longitudinal records can become highly identifying. Re-consent for changed use and allow participants to review or withdraw according to the plan.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Analyse within-person change and between-person variation. Connect moments to stages and outcomes without forcing every journey into a smooth line. The value is seeing how experience evolves after novelty, before and after consequences, and across recovery.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at design a longitudinal evidence system?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Prompts are small enough to sustain: what changed, what the person believes now, what action they took, what remains uncertain, and any artefact they wish to share. Interviews at key stages reconstruct the trajectory and clarify diary entries. Service logs provide timing and state but are never assumed to represent the lived meaning of the event.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Attrition is evidence and a validity threat. People who become unwell, lose access, resolve the problem quickly, or feel overburdened may stop responding for different reasons. The team minimises burden, offers flexible formats and compensation, records missingness, and avoids presenting only the most engaged diaries as the typical journey.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at transfer example: subscription trial?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: A launch interview captures initial enthusiasm but not habit, perceived value, billing surprise, or cancellation. A diary tied to setup, first success, lapse, renewal reminder, and charge can reveal when the product’s promise diverges from experience.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Where does the harder design decision appear?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Longitudinal research creates participant burden and sensitive data over time. Senior researchers justify every prompt, plan attrition and safeguarding, and avoid interpreting silence as success. They connect changing experience to service events rather than producing a diary of feelings without mechanism.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Can we see that in a concrete product situation?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: A budgeting app tests well in a 40-minute session. Three weeks later, people have stopped opening it because its alerts became noise and its categories no longer match changing life events. Adoption is a time-based experience.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What should I notice the next time I use a product?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Choose a service that unfolds over several days. Track when your questions change, what you forget, which reminders you create, and when waiting becomes a different experience rather than simply more time.
